title: Shares Acquires Treezor from Société Générale in BaaS Expansion
snippet: Shares has completed its purchase of Treezor to build a pan-European infrastructure group spanning payments, accounts, savings and investment. The post Shares Acquires Treezor from Société Générale in BaaS Expansion appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Shares has completed the acquisition of 100% of Treezor from Société Générale, the companies confirmed on 7 October 2026. The deal creates a combined group with regulatory licences covering electronic money, payment services, investment services and crypto-assets, supervised by the French ACPR and the AMF.

Benjamin Chemla, chief executive and co-founder of Shares Group

Benjamin Chemla, chief executive and co-founder of Shares Group, will lead the enlarged entity. Treezor will be run by Cédric Cassini, supported by Julien Mortuaire. The transaction price was not disclosed.

What each side brings

Treezor, founded in 2016 and authorised as an electronic money institution by the ACPR, has processed more than €145 billion in transaction volume and issued over 8.5 million cards since inception. It holds principal membership of both Mastercard and Visa, and its regulatory passport covers 25 EU member states. The company already generates close to 70% of its revenue growth outside France, with on-the-ground operations in Germany, Italy and Spain.

Shares began in 2021 as a retail investing application before expanding its regulated technology to serve wealth managers, financial institutions and employee savings providers. It has raised $90 million in total funding from Valar Ventures, Singular, Global Founders Capital and Red Sea Ventures, and employs around 150 people across France, the UK and Poland. Shares Financial Assets holds an ACPR-authorised investment firm licence and is registered as a crypto-asset service provider under both the ACPR and the AMF.

Together the group intends to offer a modular, white-label infrastructure stack that covers the full spectrum from current accounts and card issuance through to savings products and investment portfolios, delivered via API to fintechs, corporates and financial institutions.

“Transforming financial services in Europe requires infrastructure capable of covering the entire value chain, from accounts through to investment. This is the infrastructure we will now build together,” said Chemla.

Market context and competitive read-across

The deal lands at a meaningful moment for European Banking-as-a-Service. The first wave of BaaS providers built their businesses on accounts, cards and SEPA payments, but the commercial ceiling on that model has become visible: margins on commodity payment flows are thin, and several established platforms have faced regulatory scrutiny over the governance of their client onboarding and AML controls. The pressure is pushing the more ambitious players to either deepen their product set or consolidate with complementary capabilities.

Combining payment infrastructure with investment and savings rails is not a common move. Most BaaS providers partner with a wealthtech or savings platform through an API integration rather than bringing both inside a single regulatory perimeter. Shares and Treezor are betting that owning the full stack reduces friction for institutional clients and creates a stickier, higher-value relationship than a point-solution sale.

The regulatory dimension matters here too. Operating under MiCA for crypto-asset services, DORA for operational resilience, and MiFID II for investment products simultaneously is a compliance overhead that smaller entrants struggle to carry. For clients such as banks, insurers and large fintechs that need a fully licensed and auditable partner, that multi-licence position could be a genuine differentiator.

The near-term milestones to watch are the pace at which the combined product catalogue is unified, whether Treezor’s existing institutional clients adopt the investment and savings modules, and whether the group pursues further European licences or acquires additional capabilities to extend its geographic reach beyond its current four-country footprint.

title: UK Businesses File £700m CAT Claim over Visa and Mastercard EEA Fees
snippet: A Competition Appeal Tribunal claim alleges the card networks raised UK-EEA interchange fees five-fold after Brexit, costing businesses up to £200m a year. The post UK Businesses File £700m CAT Claim over Visa and Mastercard EEA Fees appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
A collective proceedings claim worth more than £700 million has been filed against Visa and Mastercard at the UK Competition Appeal Tribunal, alleging the two card networks exploited the removal of EU interchange caps following Brexit to levy unlawful inter-regional fees on UK businesses accepting online payments from European Economic Area customers.

The claim is brought by Ann Pope, a former Senior Director for Antitrust at the Competition and Markets Authority, acting through her vehicle Ann Pope Collective Proceedings Limited and represented by pan-European competition law firm Geradin Partners. The proposed class covers approximately 126,000 UK businesses that accepted remote payments from EEA-issued cards at any point since October 2020. Inclusion in the action is opt-out rather than opt-in, meaning businesses are automatically enrolled unless they choose to withdraw.

The fee increase at the centre of the claim

Before the end of the Brexit transition period, inter-regional interchange fees were subject to EU caps. After those caps ceased to apply to UK businesses, the Payment Systems Regulator found that Visa raised its UK-EEA online transaction fee five-fold in October 2021, moving from 0.2% to 1.15% for consumer debit cards and from 0.3% to 1.5% for consumer credit cards. Mastercard followed in April 2022 with equivalent increases.

The claim argues this was not a legitimate commercial response to changed market conditions. The UK remained part of the Single Euro Payments Area after Brexit, meaning the underlying cost structure of processing EEA-issued card transactions did not change materially. The PSR has itself concluded that Visa and Mastercard faced no effective competitive constraints on the acquiring side of their networks when setting these fees, and has proposed a price cap that remains under active consideration but has not yet been implemented.

Geradin Partners partner David Gallagher noted that the CAT had already found inter-regional interchange fee arrangements to restrict competition in a separate case. “Visa and Mastercard have great power over the payments that businesses rely on every day,” he said. “Our claims seek redress for UK businesses who, we say, have suffered harm as a result of Visa and Mastercard’s conduct.”

Market and regulatory context

The scale of potential liability reflects the economic weight of UK-EU trade. The claim cites 2025 figures showing UK exports to the EU at £384 billion, representing 41% of all UK exports. For any business selling goods or services to European consumers online, EEA-issued cards are effectively unavoidable: the PSR found Visa and Mastercard together handle nine in ten online transactions at UK businesses where the customer holds an EEA card.

The case lands at an active moment for interchange regulation in the UK. The PSR’s ongoing review of cross-border interchange, combined with the CAT’s prior findings on inter-regional fees, gives the claim a relatively firm regulatory foundation compared with many collective proceedings actions. That said, the quantum of £700 million-plus represents estimated accumulated overcharges across a broad class over several years, and final compensation, if awarded, would depend on the CAT’s assessment of the counterfactual fee level and the individual damages attributable to class members.

The action also sits within a broader European pattern. Several large-scale merchant interchange claims have proceeded before the CAT and in other EU jurisdictions over the past decade, typically on the back of prior competition authority findings. The Pope claim is notable for being filed after a domestic regulator, rather than the European Commission, identified the specific post-Brexit fee increase as problematic. That sequence may strengthen the claim’s prospects at the certification stage, though Visa and Mastercard are expected to contest both liability and the class definition.

Affected UK businesses can register interest at eeacardclaim.co.uk.

title: Ripple Prime Expands Into Prime Brokerage for Brevan Howard Funds
snippet: Ripple's institutional brokerage platform will provide multi-asset clearing and financing to the $35bn alternative investment manager. The post Ripple Prime Expands Into Prime Brokerage for Brevan Howard Funds appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Ripple has deepened its commercial relationship with Brevan Howard, the global macro and digital assets manager overseeing roughly $35 billion in assets, by extending its Ripple Prime platform to cover multi-asset prime brokerage, clearing and financing services for Brevan Howard funds. The agreement, announced on 6 October 2026, marks a material expansion beyond their existing investor relationship.

The move is notable because it converts Brevan Howard from a capital partner into an operational client. Funds managed by Brevan Howard affiliates participated in Ripple’s $500 million strategic investment round in 2025, a raise that valued Ripple at $40 billion and was led by Fortress and Citadel Securities. Having an investor of that scale also become a prime brokerage customer strengthens the commercial validation of the Ripple Prime platform considerably.

What Ripple Prime is selling

Noel Kimmel, president at Ripple Prime

Ripple Prime is positioned as a unified institutional platform spanning traditional and digital asset classes. According to the announcement, Brevan Howard will gain access to cross-asset prime services with the stated aim of improving capital efficiency and reducing operational complexity for its investment teams.

Alan McGroarty, group COO at Brevan Howard

Noel Kimmel, president of Ripple Prime, framed the deal as evidence of competitive strength in a segment he described as underserved. “There are few firms equipped to provide the next generation of prime services that sophisticated investors expect, and Brevan Howard’s trust in Ripple Prime is recognition of our strong competitive position and cross-asset capabilities,” he said.

Alan McGroarty, group COO of Brevan Howard, pointed to the convergence of traditional and digital markets as the driver. He said Ripple had built a platform that should provide investment teams with improved operational ease and capital efficiency, without elaborating on specific workflows or asset classes to be covered.

Market context and regulatory read-across

Institutional prime brokerage for digital assets is a segment that has attracted significant investment since the 2022 and 2023 market dislocations weeded out under-capitalised providers. Several traditional prime brokers, including units of major US and European banks, have stepped up digital asset clearing capabilities, while crypto-native firms have sought to build out cross-asset infrastructure to compete on breadth.

Ripple enters this space with a regulatory advantage it has spent years constructing: the company claims more than 85 licences globally, which gives it legal standing across multiple jurisdictions that newer entrants are still working to acquire. That regulatory footprint matters to a firm like Brevan Howard, which manages capital for sovereign wealth funds, pension plans and endowments that impose strict counterparty due diligence requirements.

The deal also arrives as the regulatory environment for digital asset prime services is taking clearer shape. In the US, the SEC and CFTC have been working through how existing prime brokerage rules apply to mixed traditional and digital portfolios. In the EU, MiCA introduces a harmonised framework for crypto-asset service providers that will affect how cross-border clearing arrangements are structured. Firms that can demonstrate regulatory compliance across asset classes are better placed to win mandates from the category of institutional investors that Brevan Howard represents.

The near-term markers to watch are whether Ripple Prime announces further institutional mandates on the back of this deal, the specific asset classes Brevan Howard routes through the platform, and whether Ripple pursues additional licences in jurisdictions where Brevan Howard operates, including its offices in Abu Dhabi, Singapore and Tokyo.

title: Poland and China Lead Central Bank Gold Buying Surge in 2026
snippet: Central banks collectively hold nearly 37,000 tonnes of gold, with Poland and China the year's biggest accumulators, per World Gold Council data. The post Poland and China Lead Central Bank Gold Buying Surge in 2026 appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Central banks show little sign of reducing their appetite for gold as 2026 enters its final quarter, with Poland and China leading a wave of official accumulation that underscores a structural shift in how sovereign institutions are managing reserve assets. Analysis published by investing research platform BestBrokers, drawing on World Gold Council reserve data and LBMA prices as of 6 October 2026, identifies the ten largest national buyers by tonnage through August.

Poland has added 97.8 tonnes through August, bringing its total reserves to 647.98 tonnes and putting it within 2.2 tonnes of matching its entire 2025 accumulation. The country entered the global top ten gold reserve holders earlier this year. On a per-capita basis, Poland’s holdings now equate to roughly 17.12 grams per citizen, up from the equivalent of five small gold coins per person to six, worth approximately $4,919 at current prices.

China’s buying has accelerated sharply since a slow start to the year. Monthly purchases reached 20.2 tonnes in August, described by BestBrokers as more than twenty times January’s volume. Total accumulation of 80.2 tonnes takes China’s official reserves to 2,386.55 tonnes, the world’s fifth-largest gold stockpile, valued at approximately $318.9 billion at the LBMA PM price of $4,156.40 per troy ounce recorded on 6 October.

The buyers and the sellers

Behind the two headline figures, several emerging-market and Central Asian central banks have also been consistent accumulators. Uzbekistan has added 48.2 tonnes despite two months of minor reductions, Kazakhstan has bought 36.1 tonnes with purchases in every month except January, and the Czech Republic has added gold in every single month, lifting its reserves by 14.2 tonnes to 85.76 tonnes.

The picture is not uniformly one of accumulation. Turkey has reduced its official holdings by 81.6 tonnes through August, including a 60.4-tonne reduction in March alone, making it by far the largest seller of the year. Russia has cut its reserves by 34.2 tonnes and Azerbaijan’s State Oil Fund has reduced holdings by 21.9 tonnes. Turkey briefly returned to buying in August, adding 2.9 tonnes, but remains a substantial net seller for the year.

Collectively, the world’s central banks now hold 36,888.97 tonnes of gold, equivalent to roughly 1.19 billion troy ounces.

Market context and reserve policy read-across

The BestBrokers analysis arrives as spot gold hovers near a two-month low of around $4,100 an ounce, under pressure from a stronger US dollar and elevated US Treasury yields. The macro backdrop matters for fintech and capital markets participants: gold pricing feeds directly into commodity derivatives, collateral valuations and reserve-asset modelling across institutional balance sheets.

The broader pattern of central bank buying reflects a multi-year trend that the IMF and the Bank for International Settlements have both noted in recent reserve composition surveys. A sustained shift away from dollar-denominated reserves toward physical gold is a structural consideration for currency risk management, correspondent banking relationships and cross-border payment settlement infrastructure. For payments and digital-asset practitioners specifically, any acceleration of de-dollarisation sentiment among sovereign institutions has implications for the long-term role of dollar-backed stablecoins and CBDC design choices in emerging markets.

Alan Goldberg, lead data analyst at BestBrokers, said: “Gold may be trading like a financial asset, but central banks’ buying decisions reveal something more fundamental: who wants to hold wealth in a form that cannot be printed.”

The analysis covers January to August 2026, based on data reported by central banks to the IMF and published by the World Gold Council. The next quarterly data release will indicate whether the pace of accumulation held into September.

title: ClearToken and Consensys Tie Up for 24/7 Wholesale Settlement
snippet: The pair will combine cryptographic and legal settlement finality to give banks round-the-clock delivery-versus-payment infrastructure within UK regulatory frameworks. The post ClearToken and Consensys Tie Up for 24/7 Wholesale Settlement appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
ClearToken Group and Consensys have announced a strategic partnership to deliver continuous settlement infrastructure for wholesale markets, pairing on-chain technical finality with legally binding settlement finality inside the UK regulatory perimeter.

The announcement, made in London on 8 October 2026, addresses a structural gap in tokenised-asset markets: while tokenised securities can move around the clock, the clearing, settlement and safeguarding infrastructure that wholesale institutions require has historically operated only during standard market hours. The partnership is designed to close that gap.

How the infrastructure works

Ben Santos-Stephens, CEO at ClearToken Group

ClearToken contributes two regulated entities to the arrangement. ClearToken CSD Limited holds Gate 2 approval in the Bank of England‘s Digital Securities Sandbox, which permits it to tokenise and de-tokenise eligible securities inside a financial market infrastructure’s regulatory perimeter. Its CT Register service allows eligible securities held at different banks to be recognised as a single fungible instrument; its CT Settle service extends settlement to tokenised securities on a continuous basis. ClearToken Depository Limited, authorised by the FCA as a payment institution under the Payment Services Regulations 2017, enables delivery-versus-payment settlement against fiat, tokenised deposits and stablecoins on a 24/7 basis.

David Cunningham, president at Consensys

Consensys provides the blockchain layer: the cryptographic certainty that a recorded on-chain transaction cannot be altered, along with institutional wallet infrastructure, interoperability tooling and connectivity across banking networks and financial market infrastructures. Consensys draws on more than a decade of enterprise Ethereum work, including the development of Besu, Linea and Teku, protocols that underpin several major financial institutions’ blockchain networks.

Ben Santos-Stephens, chief executive of ClearToken Group, said the partnership would give institutions the connective tissue they need to operate across multiple ledgers and networks. “Consensys brings the technology and the institutional relationships to deliver that at scale. We are building the legal and clearing framework institutions need in order to rely on it.”

David Cunningham, president of Consensys, framed the deal as a response to demand from banks and market infrastructures already moving towards always-on operations. “ClearToken is building a regulated route to clearing and settlement on a 24/7/365 basis, subject to clearing authorisation by the Bank of England. Together, this enables our clients to operate around the clock, opening up new business opportunities and reducing risk.”

ClearToken CCP Limited has separately applied to the Bank of England for authorisation as a central counterparty under UK EMIR, adding a further layer to the group’s regulatory build-out.

Regulatory and competitive context

The partnership sits squarely inside the UK’s Digital Securities Sandbox, the Bank of England and FCA’s joint framework for testing financial market infrastructure involving digital securities in a live environment. The Sandbox is designed to allow firms to explore tokenised post-trade models without immediately meeting the full requirements of existing FMI legislation, while remaining subject to conditions set out in individual approval notices.

Several other firms are pursuing similar infrastructure plays. The question of whether institutional tokenisation achieves critical mass will hinge less on the technology itself than on regulatory authorisation milestones. For ClearToken, the CCP authorisation application under UK EMIR is the next significant marker: CCP status would allow it to act as a central counterparty for cleared trades, substantially widening its addressable market and the systemic weight it carries. Until that authorisation lands, the partnership’s scope is bounded by the conditions attached to the Sandbox approval.

For Consensys, the deal extends an existing strategy of embedding its infrastructure in regulated financial market settings globally, positioning its interoperability tooling as the connective layer between bank-issued tokens, payment schemes and legacy FMIs. The durability of that positioning depends on whether Ethereum-based infrastructure retains its institutional foothold as competing networks and proprietary bank chains mature.

The FCA has conducted a major operation to disrupt a suspected organised criminal group for engaging in insider dealing and money laundering.

  

            						

On 13 October, 3 individuals were arrested following a joint operation by the FCA and the National Crime Agency (NCA). More than 100 FCA and NCA staff took part in searches at 5 residential premises in London and Manchester.

More than 30 mobile phones, laptops and tablets were seized in searches conducted by FCA investigators.

All 3 suspects are in the process of being interviewed by the FCA at police stations in London and Manchester.

Steve Smart, executive director of enforcement and market oversight at the FCA, said:

'Insider dealing is a serious threat to the integrity of our markets. Working with partners, we will continue to use all the powers at our disposal to crack down on serious and organised crime groups engaged in market abuse.'

In 2025/26, the FCA secured 4 insider dealing convictions, with 2 resulting in record sentences totalling 11 years of imprisonment. Twelve people were fined a total of £1.77m for insider dealing, market manipulation and making misleading statements.

Notes to editors

The FCA cannot comment further at this time but will provide more details when appropriate.

Fighting financial crime is a priority in the FCA’s 5-year strategy.

If you have information concerning insider dealing you can contact the FCA by phone on 0800 111 6768 or by using the FCA’s reporting form. Information can be passed confidentially.

The FCA enables a fair and thriving financial services market for the good of consumers and the economy. Find out more about the FCA.

title: Enso Brings xStocks Tokenized Equities to Arbitrum via Single API
snippet: Enso's execution infrastructure now routes xStocks on Arbitrum, letting wallets and fintechs add tokenized US equity access without new routing builds. The post Enso Brings xStocks Tokenized Equities to Arbitrum via Single API appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Enso, the Zurich-based execution infrastructure platform for onchain finance, has made xStocks available on Arbitrum through its API and RWA App. The integration means wallets, fintechs and trading platforms already connected to the Enso API can extend tokenized US equity access to Arbitrum without constructing new routing or aggregation infrastructure.

xStocks are tokenized representations of US-listed equities. By routing them through Enso’s existing execution layer, applications gain access alongside the same infrastructure already used for swaps, cross-chain routing and other DeFi actions across the networks Enso supports. Eligible users can also trade xStocks directly through the Enso RWA App within Arbitrum’s onchain ecosystem.

The distribution problem in tokenized assets

Connor Howe, co-founder and chief executive of Enso, identified what he sees as the core structural gap in real-world asset (RWA) markets. “Tokenization solved the supply side of real-world assets but what’s been missing is distribution, the liquidity, routing and execution to get those assets into the wallets and apps where people actually transact,” he said. “Bringing that to Arbitrum means any wallet, fintech or trading platform already built on Enso can offer tokenized equity access to one of Ethereum’s largest ecosystems without building anything new.”

The point is well-grounded in the current state of the market. Tokenized equity issuance has expanded materially over the past two years, but access has remained fragmented. Each new chain or venue has typically required application developers to build bespoke integrations, raising the cost and slowing adoption. Enso’s pitch is a single API that absorbs that complexity, a model it says is already powering ether.fi Cash’s tokenized stock and metals execution, an approved minting role for Ondo Finance, and the infrastructure behind Anchorage Digital’s Porto institutional terminal.

Peter Haymond, head of DeFi partnerships at Arbitrum, said real-world assets are one of the fastest-growing categories on the network and that execution infrastructure is what converts that growth into something developers can ship. The xStocks integration, he argued, is the kind of composability that compounds as more real-world assets move onchain.

Regulatory backdrop and market momentum

The timing sits against a broader wave of institutional interest in tokenized equities. The announcement noted that NYSE parent ICE and crypto exchange OKX filed with the US Securities and Exchange Commission this week for a 24/7 venue that would trade more than 60 tokenized US stocks. If approved, that would mark a significant step in legitimising tokenized equity infrastructure as a regulated asset class rather than a DeFi experiment.

In the EU, MiCA provides a framework for certain crypto-asset types, but tokenized securities remain subject to existing securities law, meaning any platform offering them to European users must navigate MiFID II compliance. In the UK, the Financial Conduct Authority‘s sandbox for digital securities is still developing clear rules. The regulatory path for tokenized equities therefore varies by jurisdiction, and Enso’s release does not specify which users are eligible to trade through the RWA App or which regulatory frameworks govern its institutional clients.

Enso says it has settled more than $22 billion onchain for more than 350 enterprise clients. The company is backed by Polychain Capital, Multicoin Capital, Spartan Group and Hypersphere, though no new funding was announced alongside this integration.

title: ABA Invests in BankTech Ventures Fund II to Back Community Banks
snippet: The American Bankers Association has taken a stake in BankTech Ventures Fund II, a community-bank-backed fund investing in early-stage bank-ready fintech The post ABA Invests in BankTech Ventures Fund II to Back Community Banks appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
The American Bankers Association (ABA) has announced an investment in BankTech Ventures Fund II, a venture fund backed by community and regional banks and focused on early-stage fintech companies building technology specifically for the banking sector. The move extends an existing venture investment strategy and reflects what the ABA describes as a sustained commitment to keeping its member institutions abreast of innovation in financial services technology.

The investment was approved by ABA’s Executive Committee, acting on a recommendation from the association’s Venture Investment Committee, which assesses opportunities aligned with the ABA’s broader mission of supporting a competitive and innovative banking industry. The ABA did not disclose the size of its commitment.

The BankTech Ventures model

Rob Nichols, president and CEO ata ABA

Founded in 2021, BankTech Ventures operates as a strategic fund rather than a purely financial one. It works with more than 125 community and regional banks, which gives the fund a direct channel into the technology decisions those institutions are making. The model is designed to generate returns for limited partners while simultaneously providing those same banks with early access to vetted vendors and the opportunity to pilot emerging products.

Carey Ransom, managing director at BankTech Ventures

ABA President and chief executive Rob Nichols said the fund’s network and its focus on bank-specific technology made it a compelling fit. “BankTech Ventures has built a strong network of community bank partners and has focused on technologies designed specifically for the banking industry,” he said. “This investment gives ABA a unique opportunity to gain early insight into emerging innovations while supporting technologies that can help banks better serve their customers.”

Carey Ransom, managing director at BankTech Ventures, said the ABA’s broad membership and industry standing made it a strategically valuable addition to Fund II’s investor base, given its reach across institutions of all sizes.

Market context

The investment reflects a structural tension that has persisted across the US community and regional banking sector for several years. Smaller institutions typically lack the technology budgets and internal development capacity of the large nationals, yet face the same competitive pressure from digital-only challengers and non-bank payment providers. Curated venture vehicles such as BankTech Ventures offer a procurement shortcut: banks receive early access to vetted tools, while portfolio companies gain warm introductions to a ready-made distribution network.

Several similar models have emerged in the US, including bank-backed innovation labs and consortium investment vehicles, though BankTech Ventures is one of the more structured standalone funds operating at this segment of the market. The ABA’s involvement adds a layer of institutional credibility and reach that could influence which vendors get traction across its member base of small, regional and large banks collectively holding $26.5 trillion in assets.

The move also mirrors a trend in European banking, where banking associations and savings bank groups have taken equity stakes in fintech accelerators and funds as a means of supplementing their members’ innovation capacity without requiring each institution to run its own venture programme.

For the fintech companies in BankTech Ventures’ pipeline, the ABA’s entry as an investor carries potential distribution value beyond capital. Access to the association’s conferences, standards-setting work and regulatory engagement could accelerate product adoption in a market segment where trust and familiarity with the vendor’s backing often matters as much as the technology itself. The next markers to watch are the size of the ABA’s commitment once disclosed and the specific technology verticals Fund II prioritises.

title: Capitolis Closes $220m Financing to Acquire eSecLending
snippet: The capital markets fintech raised a $120m Series E at a $1.9bn valuation, led by Citi, to fund its $200m all-cash purchase of The post Capitolis Closes $220m Financing to Acquire eSecLending appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Capitolis has completed $220 million in financing, comprising a $120 million Series E equity round valued at $1.9 billion and an accompanying debt facility, to fund its acquisition of eSecLending in a separate $200 million all-cash transaction announced the previous week.

The equity round was led by Citi, an existing investor. New strategic investors joining the cap table include Bank of America, Nomura and Tradeweb Markets. Existing investors Barclays, BNP Paribas, J.P. Morgan, State Street and UBS also participated. The debt portion is being provided by First Citizens Innovation Banking (formerly Silicon Valley Bank), Hercules Capital and Pinegrove Venture Partners.

The deal

The rationale for the eSecLending acquisition sits squarely in Capitolis’ core pitch: reducing the capital and balance sheet burden on the large bank-dealers it counts as both investors and clients. Capitolis already operates a Capital Marketplace and a Portfolio Optimization business, both of which aim to help financial institutions net down exposures, redeploy collateral and free up regulatory capital. Adding securities lending extends that logic into a market that has historically been operationally intensive and, as Serene Murphy, global head of corporate development at Tradeweb, noted in the announcement, reliant on manual processes.

“Securities lending represents the next frontier in the electronification we’ve seen across our markets, and Capitolis’ acquisition of eSecLending will be an important step in that evolution,” Murphy said. “By combining eSecLending’s network of institutional asset owners with Capitolis’ financial resource optimisation platform, this deal creates real opportunities to bring more automation and efficiency to a market that has historically relied on manual processes.”

The strategic significance of eSecLending’s institutional asset owner network is also material. Securities lending programmes are a significant source of incremental return for large pension funds, sovereign wealth funds and asset managers; access to that network gives Capitolis a distribution channel that complements its existing bank-dealer relationships.

Market context

Gil Mandelzis, founder and CEO at Capitolis

Capitolis operates in a segment that has attracted serious institutional backing precisely because bank balance sheet optimisation is not a cyclical priority but a structural one. Under the Basel III endgame framework and its various national implementations, large banks face continued pressure on leverage ratios and risk-weighted assets. Technology that demonstrably reduces those burdens commands durable commercial value, which explains why the investor roster reads like a who’s who of global capital markets franchises rather than a typical venture syndicate.

The involvement of Tradeweb as both a strategic investor and a voice for the electronification thesis is notable. Tradeweb has built a substantial electronic fixed-income and derivatives platform, and its public endorsement of the securities lending automation angle adds credibility to the commercial opportunity Capitolis is staking out.

Competition in capital optimisation technology is real: several established vendors and internal bank initiatives operate in portfolio compression, netting and collateral management. Capitolis’ differentiator has been its multi-dealer network effect, where the value of the platform rises as more bank participants use it to identify offsetting positions. Adding a securities lending layer deepens that network and raises the switching cost for participants already embedded in the system.

Founder and chief executive Gil Mandelzis described the Series E as a strong endorsement of Capitolis’ vision and ability to execute. FT Partners served as the exclusive strategic and financial adviser to Capitolis on the transaction.

title: Oobit Lets AI Assistants Pay with Stablecoins Via One-Time Cards
snippet: Oobit AI Payments issues a disposable card per transaction, letting AI agents spend stablecoins without accessing the user's underlying account. The post Oobit Lets AI Assistants Pay with Stablecoins Via One-Time Cards appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Oobit, a Singapore-based stablecoin payments firm, has launched Oobit AI Payments, a product that lets users authorise AI assistants to make purchases on their behalf using stablecoins, without granting those assistants access to the underlying account balance or primary payment credentials.

Amram Adar, co-founder and CEO at Oobit

The mechanism works through ephemeral card issuance. When a user asks an AI assistant to book, buy or pay for something, the assistant flags the transaction for approval. Once the user confirms, Oobit generates a one-time virtual card tied exclusively to that transaction. The AI receives the card details it needs to complete checkout; it never holds the user’s wallet credentials or sees the broader account. Oobit then handles identity verification, authorisation and payment execution in the background.

The product supports USDT and other stablecoins. Users in supported markets can also fund their Oobit balance through local payment rails, including bank transfers, mobile money networks and Brazil’s Pix instant payment system. The company says the solution is available across more than 75 countries.

“AI can already understand what you want and figure out how to get it,” said Amram Adar, co-founder and CEO of Oobit. “The missing piece is the ability to pay. That shouldn’t depend on where you live or which bank card you have.”

The architecture of delegated payments

Oobit’s core design choice, separating permission to pay from access to money, addresses a genuine structural problem in agentic AI commerce. As large language model platforms move from information retrieval into task execution, the question of how an AI agent interacts with financial accounts becomes a live compliance and consumer-protection issue. Unrestricted wallet access creates risks around unauthorised transactions, account takeover and liability attribution that neither banks nor regulators have fully resolved.

The one-time card model is not new in isolation. Virtual card infrastructure has been used in accounts-payable automation, B2B procurement and travel expense management for years. What Oobit is doing is applying that architecture to the consumer-facing AI agent context and running it on top of stablecoin settlement rather than traditional card rails. Whether the underlying settlement is genuinely on-chain or whether Oobit abstracts that into a fiat-equivalent flow for the merchant is not specified in the announcement.

Market context and regulatory read-across

Several payments and crypto firms are positioning for agentic commerce. Visa and Mastercard have both signalled interest in credentialing AI agents for payment execution, while a number of crypto-native firms are exploring stablecoin-based payment APIs for developer integration. Oobit’s differentiation appears to rest on its cross-border reach through local payment rails and its focus on users whose funds originate in digital assets rather than bank accounts.

The regulatory landscape is still forming. In the EU, the revised Payment Services Directive (PSD3) and the accompanying Payment Services Regulation will tighten requirements around delegated payment access and strong customer authentication, which is directly relevant to any model where a third-party agent initiates transactions. In the UK, the FCA‘s ongoing work on payments supervision similarly touches on authorised access and fraud liability. Oobit will need to demonstrate how its per-transaction approval model satisfies authentication standards across the jurisdictions it serves.

title: Stablecoin startups advance payments
snippet: Entrepreneurs embracing the digital assets are pushing payments modernization forward, and bringing incumbents along too.
fullText:
Fintech entrepreneurs are using stablecoins as a means of breaking into the payments industry and driving digital modernization.

Startups such as MassPay and Rain have been forging new pathways for payments that embrace stablecoins, either incorporating or bypassing aging rails. They see an expansive opportunity ahead as they begin to make inroads.

While traditional payments players, including card network giant Visa and mega processor Fiserv, have also glommed on to the stablecoin trend, their legacy infrastructures may increase the difficulty of adapting to digital schemes.

Meanwhile, younger companies are amassing capital from venture investors and hiring employees to build stablecoin networks and accessories. The appeal for investors has been a simple one, according to Verda Ventures General Partner Alex Witt.

“The basic premise behind our fund is: sending payments should be as easy, fast, and cheap as sending a text message,” Witt said in an interview this month. “We fundamentally believe with blockchain, mobile phones, and the internet, that is completely possible.”

Witt and his business partner, Amit Chu, created a venture fund two years ago to invest in stablecoin startups and it has since drawn $40 million, he said, allowing the fund to purchase minority stakes in about two dozen companies globally. 

It’s a real change from when Witt first started to raise money for the fund in 2024 and people thought he was “completely crazy,” he said.

The Verda portfolio includes the fintech Yellow Card focused on payments in Africa as well as the blockchain infrastructure services company Capa, which operates in Latin America.

Two other companies the fund invested in have already been sold, specifically Kulipa and Beam. In addition, digital processor Stripe is circling another possible purchase, Witt said, declining to name it.

Rain evolves into stablecoin services

Rain’s holding company, Signify, began as a different business and then morphed into the one branded as Rain today. It has collected about $338 million in equity investments along the way, according to a spokesperson for the company. 

Among the private company’s investors are San Francisco investment firm Iconiq Capital, Sapphire Ventures and Coinbase’s former chief technology officer, Balaji Srinivasan, with a quarter of a billion dollars raised in the most recent round disclosed in January.

Rain provides stablecoin infrastructure services that enable corporate customers to bridge stablecoin payments so that money can move from the digital assets to traditional payment rails. Corporate clients embed the technology in their services for consumer use, letting consumers tap stablecoins in a way that’s less invisible to users. 

Early clients were crypto firms, fintechs and neobanks, sometimes in countries where the digital assets acted as a hedge against inflation, such as in Argentina. But then Rain began attracting bigger names, landing remittance provider Western Union as its first major customer last year, then a large peer, MoneyGram, and ticketing company Live Nation followed this year.

This week, Rain said it’s making a digital wallet available to consumers that will enable them to save, spend and send from a stablecoin balance that is backed by cards the company issues. For now, consumers will still custody their funds with the non-custodial wallets, but the company plans to offer custodial wallets by yearend.

Rain expands following Genius Act

Rain has grown by acquisition too. In August, Rain purchased the California payments and technology firm Ansa for an undisclosed sum. 

Now, the business employs about 150 people around the world, with a pack of them located in the New York headquarters, the company’s CEO, Farooq Malik, said in an interview last month.

The brand name Rain dawned on the founders because they saw how fast and fluid funds could be transferred using stablecoins. The same could be said for how quickly startup businesses are reacting to stablecoin developments, like the signing of the Genius Act, which created a regulatory framework for the digital assets.

President Donald Trump’s signing of that new law last year was pivotal in pushing the business forward, Malik said.

“The tipping point was really the Genius Act,” he said. “A lot of people had been waiting on the sidelines for clarity before proceeding. That gave companies and people the confidence to proceed. Consumers also have to believe this is viable.”

Now, the company aims to take another step in its evolution. It applied with the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency for a national trust charter this month, seeking the ability to offer asset custody and other related services, though they could still accept deposits or make loans. 

MassPay embraces stablecoins

Another startup growing in the stablecoin arena is Las Vegas-based MassPay, which is using the digital asset technology to streamline payments for gig workers, contractors and marketplace sellers as well as providing payout services for gaming and sports betting. It connects to local payment rails, real-time payment systems and mobile wallets.

“We've seen growing demand for stablecoins, primarily by large-scale institutions that feel comfortable due to some clearance in the regulation,” the company’s CEO, Ran Grushkowsky, said in an interview last month. Stablecoins are becoming particularly useful for speed and payments over the weekends, he explained.

The majority of MassPay’s 300 corporate clients are in North America, Grushkowsky said. They include Los Angeles-based online social platform Passes and New York-based marketplace Whop.

Last week, MassPay said it had forged a new integration with Block’s Cash App digital wallet.

MassPay’s services are offered in some 230 countries, according to the press release last December that named Grushkowsky CEO as of this year. The company has grown to process tens of billions of dollars annually, with about half of those payments moving across borders, and about 10% in stablecoins, he said.

The company is privately funded, and now employs about 54 workers, mainly in the U.S., Grushkowsky said. He declined to say how much money the owners have raised. 

As startups nudge stablecoins forward, the digital currency is slowly becoming a real possibility for payments in everyday life, Witt explained. 

“The biggest challenge, though, is that last mile of friction and localizing to consumer preferences,” Witt said. “We wanted to invest in the leaders around the world that are bridging the gap.”

Victims of a £1.5m crypto investment fraud will recover lost funds after the FCA obtained confiscation orders against Raymondip Bedi and Patrick Mavanga.

  

            						

At a hearing at Southwark Crown Court on 28 September 2026, Raymondip Bedi was ordered to pay £603,404.28 and Patrick Mavanga £247,997.99.

Between February 2017 and June 2019, Bedi and Mavanga operated a fraudulent investment scheme, cold-calling consumers and persuading them to invest in fake cryptoasset opportunities through companies including CCX Capital and Astaria Group LLP. At least 65 investors were defrauded and lost £1,541,799.

The FCA has identified and contacted victims of the fraud and will ensure that funds recovered through the confiscation process are returned to victims.

In July 2025, following an FCA prosecution, Raymondip Bedi was sentenced to 5 years and 4 months' imprisonment and Patrick Mavanga was sentenced to 6 years and 6 months' imprisonment for their roles in the scheme.

Steve Smart, joint executive director of enforcement and market oversight at the FCA, said:

'Bedi and Mavanga defrauded investors and left them out of pocket. These orders bring victims a step closer to getting money back.

'We’ll keep coming after fraudsters and holding them to account.'

Notes to editors

Raymondip Bedi’s date of birth is 9 October 1989.

Patrick Mavanga’s date of birth is 24 November 1984.

FCA secures convictions against two individuals for £1.5m fraud.

Two individuals sentenced to a combined 12 years for £1.5m crypto fraud.

title: SBI, Mesh Connect and Money Forward Form Digital-Asset JV in Japan
snippet: The three firms have agreed to establish Mesh SBI Money Forward Network KK to build API-connected digital asset payment infrastructure in Japan. The post SBI, Mesh Connect and Money Forward Form Digital-Asset JV in Japan appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
SBI Holdings, Mesh Connect and Money Forward have signed a basic agreement to establish a joint venture in Japan targeting the fragmented digital asset connectivity market. The entity, to be named Mesh SBI Money Forward Network KK, is planned for launch in 2026 and will focus primarily on the Japanese market, subject to definitive agreements, internal approvals and engagement with relevant regulatory authorities.

The ownership structure gives Mesh Connect, the California-headquartered API connectivity provider, a 60% controlling stake. SBI Group will hold 26% and Money Forward 14%, reflecting the existing shareholder relationship Money Forward already holds in Mesh. The joint venture’s stated business purpose is the expansion of crypto-asset service provider (CASP) activity in Japan.

What the joint venture will do

The three parties have identified four initial business areas for the venture to assess. These are: account connectivity and digital asset transfers between exchanges, wallets and other services; streamlined procedures for buying, transferring and using digital assets; payment solutions using crypto assets and stablecoins; and infrastructure services enabling tokenised assets and digital payments for financial institutions. The release characterises current workflows as fragmented, with users forced to navigate multiple platforms with inconsistent connectivity.

Mesh’s core product is an API layer that connects crypto asset exchanges, wallets and payment platforms. The company says it already has integrations across numerous services globally. The joint venture is designed to bring that connectivity infrastructure to Japan using SBI Group’s domestic regulatory expertise and financial services relationships, while Money Forward contributes management support and its existing stake in Mesh.

Over a longer horizon, the venture plans to consider expansion into stablecoin connectivity and tokenised asset payment rails, which the companies framed as building interoperability between digital assets, stablecoins, tokenised assets and fiat currency.

Market and regulatory context

Japan is one of the few major economies with a mature, purpose-built regulatory framework for crypto asset service providers, administered by the Financial Services Agency (FSA). The country has operated a crypto exchange registration regime since 2017 and has continued to refine its rules around stablecoins and payment tokens, including amendments that came into force in 2023 establishing a distinct legal category for electronic payment instruments. That regime makes Japan a relatively attractive jurisdiction for structured digital asset infrastructure plays, because the compliance path is defined even if it is demanding.

SBI Holdings is a substantial presence in Japanese financial services and has maintained a long-standing strategic interest in digital assets, including through its association with Ripple and its own crypto exchange operations. Money Forward is a well-established Japanese financial software business focused on accounting and personal finance tools, giving the venture a route into the SME and consumer segments where digital asset adoption is still nascent.

The competitive context in Japan includes domestic exchange operators and several global platforms with FSA registration. The joint venture’s differentiator, if the business model proves out, would be the connectivity layer rather than custody or exchange services, which positions it as infrastructure for the existing licensed players rather than a direct competitor to them. Whether Japanese exchange operators and wallet providers are willing to connect via a third-party API layer will be the central commercial question. The presence of SBI as a shareholder and a known regulatory actor may ease those conversations.

The FCA and Practitioner Panel annual survey of regulated firms provides valuable insights into how firms think we’re performing.

The latest survey shows 79% of firms are highly satisfied with their relationship with the FCA, up from 74% last year. The proportion of firms rating the FCA as a highly effective regulator also increased from 69% to 76%, while 75% reported high levels of trust.

Firms were most confident in our work to protect consumers (87%), ensure markets work well (85%) and enhance the integrity of the UK financial system (85%). There was a 27-percentage point increase in firms’ understanding of the Secondary International Competitiveness and Growth Objective and a 25-percentage point increase in confidence in our delivery of it.

We took on board feedback from last year’s survey and provided further guidance to help firms embed the Consumer Duty. This year, 88% of firms say they understand what we expect on supporting consumers and embedding the Duty.

The findings also provide valuable insight into where firms would like to see further progress, including on regulatory burden. We’re already simplifying reporting by removing outdated or duplicated data returns for 90% of firms.

Nikhil Rathi, chief executive of the FCA, said: 'A year into our strategy it's encouraging to see growing confidence across many areas of our work. We know there is more to do. For example, while we can’t do our job without the data firms provide, we should continue to simplify requests and make them easier to manage.'

Matt Hammerstein, chair of the FCA Practitioner Panel, said: 'This year’s survey results indicate firms continue to have broadly positive views of the FCA, including strong understanding of expectations under the Consumer Duty and significant growth in confidence in the FCA’s ability to deliver on its secondary objectives focused on growth and competitiveness.

'The Panel is encouraging the FCA to be clearer about the outcomes it expects its priorities to produce, and more vocal about the progress it is making against these, to strengthen confidence in the UK as a leading global financial centre and attractive place to invest.'

In the first year of our strategy, we've delivered an estimated £5.6bn in benefits to consumers and the economy, including launching My FCA, reducing reporting burdens to save firms around £16m annually, and introducing nearly 50 pro-growth measures to boost UK competitiveness and innovation. 

Since the survey was conducted, we’ve continued our work to deliver landmark reforms, including working with HM Treasury and the Financial Ombudsman Service to modernise the redress framework, support industry delivery of the Advice Guidance Boundary Review, regulating Buy Now Pay Later products, establishing a new regime for cryptoassets, and progressing the PISCES private markets framework.

fullText:
Speech by Jon Relleen, director of infrastructure and exchanges, at the Reform of the UK Public and Private Capital Markets Summit 2026.

  

Speaker: Jon Relleen, director of infrastructure and exchanges 

Event: Reform of the UK Public and Private Capital Markets Summit 2026

Delivered: 5 October 2026  

Note: This is a drafted speech and may differ from the delivered version

Reading time: 9 minutes

Highlights:

The FCA’s wide-ranging reforms over recent years are making UK capital markets more effective, competitive and attractive.

Trust, market integrity and high standards set the foundations for sustainable growth, and it is crucial that we also enable informed risk-taking.

We’re preparing for tomorrow’s markets by supporting innovation, including tokenisation.

    

            						

The Economic Secretary to the Treasury has discussed the contribution of UK markets to economic growth. 

I want to build on that by talking about the FCA’s role in reforming capital market rules.

The headline is that we've been very busy over the past few years. 

We’ve now completed major aspects of a multi-year programme of work, to ensure capital markets work well for our economy and support growth.

This has already delivered positive changes. But there’s plenty more to come.

We are working on further reforms, while also adapting to rapid changes in markets and use of technology.

In fact, areas such as tokenisation, AI and markets for trading private company shares have become central to our capital markets policy programme. 

And that tells us something important. As markets change, our approach has had to change too.

The question has not been whether regulation changes. It has been how we adjust in a way that preserves trust while also supporting innovation and growth.

Let me start by talking about our approach to the work.

We have been working with the Treasury, the Bank of England and in close dialogue with the private sector, on a raft of wholesale market reforms.

These draw on formal reports, like the Wholesale Markets Review, our process of reviewing inherited EU regulation, and issues raised by market contacts.

Some have suggested the work programme is a list not a strategy. But I think that underestimates it. There are some key principles running through it.

          

            						

Reforming from a position of strength

First, we are reforming from a position of strength, by building on the UK’s advantages.

The UK is home to deep, trusted and internationally connected capital markets. 

London continues to rank among the world’s leading financial centres. Our markets are respected and characterised by strong institutions and a reputation for integrity.

And the UK offers a full range of markets and services, supported by a diverse system of issuers, investors, intermediaries and infrastructure.

So our work programme is broad too. Covering primary markets, secondary markets, post-trade arrangements and a broad range of assets.

But successful markets cannot stand still.

Capital is increasingly mobile. Technology is reshaping markets. Private markets have grown. And new forms of trading and market infrastructure are emerging.

So our challenge is to preserve these strengths, whilst keeping UK markets dynamic and internationally competitive.

          

            						

Rebalancing risk

In some areas this requires us to think differently about regulation.

For a while, financial regulation became more detailed and prescriptive. Often for understandable reasons following periods of market stress.

But we know that growth, innovation and investment all depend on taking risk.

That is why our approach is founded on the principle of maintaining high standards while creating more space for informed risk-taking and innovation. 

This is especially relevant in wholesale markets, where professional participants assess opportunities and weigh risks every day.

Our role is to create regulation that enables this through clear rules and good disclosures, so that firms and investors can make informed decisions.

This is what we mean when we talk about rebalancing risk.

It does not mean lowering standards or weakening market integrity.

It means being deliberate about where regulation is needed and where market participants can take decisions themselves, armed with good information and appropriate disclosures.

In many cases, that means we can shift away from detailed prescription towards outcomes, transparency and accountability.

In doing so, we must never forget the underlying objective.

Ultimately, we want companies to have good options for how to raise capital, so they can invest and grow. And investors to have access to a broad range of investment opportunities.

Regulation cannot, on its own, drive economic growth. But good regulation and markets that work well are vital for a healthy economy.

          

            						

Turning reform into results

You can see our approach in the reforms we have already delivered.

We have completed around 30 capital-markets focused workstreams. And there’s an even larger number across the FCA’s broader work.

That’s too many to discuss individually in this speech. There’s a list below, but to summarise some of them:

In primary markets, we introduced once-in-a-generation changes to the UK listing regime, significantly reducing costs for issuers and supporting competitiveness with other jurisdictions. Since then, we have seen many corporate transactions that have been simplified as a result. And around 25 companies have joined the Main Market, including 7 IPOs in H1 2026.

Our new public offers framework raised the thresholds for when prospectuses are needed by companies raising capital and we also introduced public offer platforms to facilitate off-market fundraising. We have already seen a rise in capital raised by companies, including via debt markets, alongside the broader benefits of a simpler and more flexible regime.

In secondary markets, we have significantly improved transparency in bond and derivatives markets. This includes the bond consolidated tape, which launched in June – the first consolidated tape outside North America – which already has 1.6 million licences subscribed to it. These changes are shining a new light on UK markets, delivering a 70% increase in corporate bond trades and 30% for government bond trades observed in real time and enhancing the way market participants view the market.

We are moving towards an equity consolidated tape too and will appoint a provider next year. In the meantime, we launched a market activity report, so investors see the true scale of UK equity trading.

We have also responded to the growth of private markets through the creation of PISCES, a new market for trading in private company shares. Four operators have been authorised and we’ve seen seven transactions – involving companies ranging from tech firms, to brewers and board-game makers.

In post-trade, we’ve adjusted transaction reporting, with initial proposals estimated to save firms £100m per year.

And we’ve altered some of the clearing and margining rules, including increasing the clearing threshold for commodity derivatives following volatility in commodity markets.

On the investor side, we are streamlining regulatory requirements for the asset management sector, via the AIFMD review, and supporting the government in its review of the pension market.

We’re also supporting retail participation by improving access to investment advice and simplifying product information.

And our changes to primary market rules have positively impacted retail investment. We’ve seen a 50% increase in the value of retail-denominated corporate bonds and an increase in domestic retail investor allocation in fundraisings.

We are not done though.

A range of further reforms are planned or underway.

For example, on securitisation markets; listed company disclosures; benchmarks; and rules on clearing and margining.

We’re always in listening mode. So if you have ideas that would benefit UK markets please tell us.

          

            						

Competitiveness without compromise

We are doing this work to make markets work better, which is our statutory objective.

By doing that, we support growth and international competitiveness.

Capital is mobile. Businesses have choices about where they raise finance, invest and operate. The UK cannot ignore that reality.

But competitiveness does not come from a race to the bottom.

The UK's reputation for openness, stability and high standards is a strategic asset.

Our approach is pragmatic. We will challenge inherited rules when they no longer serve markets effectively, learn from other jurisdictions, and recognise the value of international consistency.

But we will do so without compromising market integrity, which provides the bedrock for sustainable growth.

          

            						

Preparing for tomorrow’s markets

I want to finish by talking about how we’re preparing for tomorrow’s markets.

We want to support innovation. To ensure markets evolve and use technology that opens up opportunities, efficiencies and encourages new entrants.

One example is working with firms to support the safe and responsible adoption of AI. Through our AI Lab, the AI Consortium with the Bank, and innovation sandboxes that allow firms to test ideas with us. 

And we are enabling firms and markets to explore tokenisation.

With the Bank and Treasury, we set up the Digital Securities Sandbox, which will support issuance of the new digital gilt (or DIGIT) early next year. Many think that the success of DIGIT can catalyse digital activity in UK.

We have worked with industry on new rules and governance for tokenised investment funds and the launch of the UK’s first fully-native tokenised fund.

And with Treasury and the Bank we’ve developed a regulatory framework for stablecoins.

But we are at a critical point. Keeping pace with other jurisdictions will require effective coordination between the private and public sectors. Industry leadership will be at least as important as public policy. 

Firms need to build, scale and innovate, moving beyond pilots to demonstrate real commercial use.

The UK’s Wholesale Digital Markets Champion, Chris Woolard, is playing a key role in coordinating the sector.

We know that regulatory clarity matters too. That’s why in May we published a joint vision with the Bank of England, setting out the regulatory principles for tokenised wholesale markets.

The feedback was clear. Industry wants to move quickly. In turn, we will provide certainty in areas such as prudential treatment, custody and market infrastructure.

We share the sense of urgency.

In coming weeks we will publish a joint roadmap, setting out how the UK’s wholesale markets will adapt as we work collectively to realise the benefits from tokenisation and digitalization.

Our objective is not to predict exactly what future markets will look like.

It is to ensure that our regulatory framework can adapt as markets evolve.

          

            						

Conclusion

We want UK capital markets to remain among the most trusted in the world, whilst also being among the most innovative, competitive and attractive. Markets that allow businesses to raise capital, help investors, and support the wider economy.

Our wide-ranging reforms have already delivered positive outcomes, across a variety of markets.

The approach is to build on the UK’s strengths and enable informed risk-taking, while preserving the trust, integrity and high standards on which successful markets depend.

The programme of reform will continue to evolve as markets change.

But the direction is clear. We are building markets that are ready not only for today's economy but for tomorrow's as well.

title: Upgrade applies for ILC charter
snippet: The decade-old credit-card startup named a SoFi alum and longtime regulator as CEO of its proposed bank.
fullText:
Upgrade has applied for an industrial loan company charter with the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp. and the Nevada Financial Institutions Division, the fintech announced Monday.

“We are excited at the prospect of establishing a new bank that will advance Upgrade’s mission of bringing responsible and affordable credit to consumers,” Virginia Varela, proposed CEO of Upgrade Bank, said in a statement. 

Varela brings more than 40 years of experience in the banking sector – first, as a regulator. She spent more than two decades with the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, and another two years as a senior bank examiner with the Federal Reserve, before specializing in bank turnarounds after the 2007-08 financial crisis, according to her LinkedIn profile.

Varela was CEO of Sacramento, California-based Golden Pacific Bank when SoFi bought the lender. She became head of SoFi’s community banking unit but left in July 2025 for Upgrade, where she is head of banking strategy.

Varela will serve on Upgrade Bank’s board alongside Upgrade co-founder and CFO Jeffrey Bogan, the company said. Raymond Specht, onetime CEO of Toyota Financial Savings Bank, will serve as an independent director on the board.

Upgrade launched roughly a decade ago offering personal loans but gradually expanded to encompass credit cards, mobile banking, auto financing and buy now, pay later. The fintech has delivered about $53 billion in credit to roughly 8.5 million customers, it said.

Upgrade counts Cross River and Celtic Bank as partners on loans, credit lines and banking services. An ILC charter would make Upgrade less dependent on those relationships.

Trump-era regulators have seen a sharp increase in new charter applications. FDIC Chair Travis Hill last year touted the ILC charter as one of a handful of ways to boost the establishment of new banks.

Rent fintech Flex and BNPL juggernaut Klarna Group applied for ILC charters in July. Car maker Stellantis received approval in May to launch an ILC. Other automotive stalwarts, including Ford and General Motors, got green lights in January. Investment firm Edward Jones followed in February. 

Some lawmakers, with backing from the banking industry, have argued that an ILC charter exempts companies from the definition of a “bank” under the Bank Holding Company Act. As long as ILCs don’t offer demand deposit accounts, they can bypass oversight by the Federal Reserve, the politicians contend.

The trade group Independent Community Bankers of America said in May that cutting the Fed out of ILC supervision “leav[es] a dangerous gap in safety and soundness oversight and introducing unnecessary systemic risk into the banking system.”

Last year, Sens. Elizabeth Warren, D-MA, and Andy Kim, D-NJ, proposed a moratorium on commercially owned ILC charters until such entities are defined as “banks” under the BHC Act.

title: Businesses view stablecoins warily
snippet: Despite the hype surrounding the digital assets, businesses remain cool to using the cryptocurrency, according to the results of a Cleveland Federal Reserve survey.
fullText:
Stablecoins aren’t going to become a disruptive force in payments in the United States anytime soon as businesses are displaying a lack of enthusiasm for the digital currency, based on a survey by the Cleveland Federal Reserve Bank.

Reasons businesses are cool to using stablecoins include lack of familiarity with the technology; satisfaction with legacy payment options; and little to no demand among customers and suppliers to use stablecoins for payment, according to the results of the Cleveland Fed’s survey in late September.

Of the survey’s 148 respondents, only one said it is currently using stablecoins. Among the remaining respondents, seven said they plan to use stablecoins in the future. The other respondents either said they weren’t sure they would use stablecoins in the future or expressed a lack of familiarity with the digital currency.

The results were somewhat surprising to Federal Reserve researchers conducting the survey as they expected more respondents to have plans to begin using stablecoins. 

“We didn’t expect the results to be as lopsided as they were,” Peter Zimmerman, a research economist for the Cleveland Fed who co-authored the report, said in summarizing the survey’s results during an interview earlier this month. 

Lack of knowledge about stablecoins is a big reason why businesses are not rushing to accept them for payment or use stablecoins for payment, according to the Cleveland Fed’s report. 

When asked what factors would influence their decision to use stablecoins, 49 respondents, about a third, cited the need for more time to observe market trends and adoption. 

While respondents were not “terribly critical” of stablecoins in their comments, many said they needed “more time to understand the technology,” Zimmerman said.

The Federal Reserve of Cleveland conducted its research in September 2025, about two months after the Genius Act became law, providing a federal regulatory framework for stablecoin payments. The Federal Reserve of Cleveland surveyed companies in the Fourth Federal Reserve District, which includes Ohio, western Pennsylvania, eastern Kentucky, and the northern panhandle of West Virginia.

One reason businesses may lack knowledge about stablecoins and potential use cases for the digital currency is that they are primarily being used for back-end settlement between banks, which keeps the technology in the background.

“What we are seeing is stablecoins being linked to cards for payments, which on the front end looks like a normal card transaction,” said Aaron McPherson, principal of AFM Consulting, in an interview this month. “Banks settle those transactions in stablecoins on the back-end between themselves, but the public doesn’t see that. What they see is the front-end of the transaction.”

Another roadblock to stablecoins becoming a mainstream payment option is the efficiency, cost effectiveness and competitiveness of existing payment options in the U.S., such as the ACH network. Some 42 survey respondents, just under a third of those surveyed, said they need more evidence stablecoins are cheaper or more efficient than other forms of payment.

“Any new payment option clearly has to be better than the existing options to break the inertia,” McPherson said. “There is a cost of acceptance for stablecoins, like other payment options, but stablecoins don’t have a clear economic advantage over many established payment methods yet.”

Lack of demand from customers to pay with stablecoins is also a barrier for businesses to accept or pay with stablecoins. Among respondents to the Cleveland Fed’s survey, 50, or about a third, said consumer demand to accept stablecoins for payment is a key factor influencing their decision to use stablecoins.

“To get people to want to pay with stablecoins, they need an inducement to do so, such as earning rewards,” McPherson said.

McPherson likens the situation to the chicken and egg scenario with any new payment option: acceptance drives usage and vice versa. “Inducing demand to spend stablecoins will boost acceptance,” McPherson added.

Despite the many headwinds facing stablecoins as a payment option, the best use case for the digital currency is cross-border payments, say some industry consultants. Using stablecoins for cross-border payments enables funds to move directly between the sender’s and recipient’s digital wallet, which reduces the number of parties involved in the transaction, lowers fees and speeds the transaction.

“In the U.S., stablecoins are largely a niche payment option and their best use case is cross-border payments,” Tony DeSanctis, vice president for Cornerstone Advisors, said in an interview this month. “Businesses that have a lot of international clients is where we will see activity.”

If businesses are going to overcome their lack of enthusiasm for using stablecoins, they need an answer to the question of how stablecoins will improve operations.

“Businesses need to be educated about what the technology is capable of, [to understand] whether it can disrupt the current state of payments and find the niche where it can serve,” DeSanctis said. “No one knows for sure what technology will be the next market disruptor, but we haven’t seen enough of stablecoins to make that distinction.”

We asked the Court to make Arthur Temlett, trading as Abacus Insurance Consultants ('Abacus'), bankrupt. This is known as sequestration in Scotland. The Sheriff granted our application on 27 August 2026.

  

            						

Emma Porter of Aver Chartered Accountants ('Aver') was appointed as trustee. She will now assess Mr Temlett’s financial affairs and seek to distribute any recovered funds to creditors.

Arthur Temlett is awaiting trial on embezzlement charges brought following an investigation by Police Scotland.

On 21 January 2025, we took action to protect consumers by stopping Arthur Temlett from carrying out any regulated activities, including acting as an insurance broker. This was because of concerns that he may have sold home and motor insurance without passing premium payments on to the insurance provider.

          

            						

  

Who to contact if you’re a customer

Customers of Abacus can contact the trustee, at Aver on:

Telephone: 0330 555 6155

Email: [email protected]

Address: PO Box 24213, Edinburgh EH1 9AT 

          

        

Information for customers 

    

      

      						I purchased home or car insurance from Abacus, what should I do?
			
    

    

						

As Abacus stopped regulated activities in January 2025, we expect that most previous policies will have expired or been renewed with another provider by now. However, if customers are concerned, they should contact their insurance providers directly to check that their insurance is valid and in place. If they are uninsured, they should arrange alternative cover immediately.

Alternative insurance can be bought directly from an insurance firm or arranged via an insurance broker. The British Insurance Brokers’ Association offers a service for customers who need help finding an authorised broker.

Anyone who believes they have paid for a policy that does not exist should report this to Police Scotland in the first instance by dialling 101 and using the crime reference number: CR/0470100/24.

Customers should also contact the trustee, using the contact details above. The trustee will explain to you what to do if you are affected.

			

  

      

      						I have an existing complaint at Abacus, what happens now?
			
    

    

						

If you’ve made a complaint against Abacus, you may have a claim if you are due any money in compensation.

You should contact the trustee for more details on how complaints or claims will be dealt with, using the contact details above.

			

  

      

      						What is the Financial Services Compensation Scheme (FSCS)?
			
    

    

						

The Financial Services Compensation Scheme (FSCS) protects consumers when UK financial services firms go out of business.

Whether you’re covered by the FSCS will depend on:

The firm.

Type of activity the firm does.

The FSCS is operationally independent of the FCA. The FSCS decides whether compensation is payable under our compensation rules.

			

  

      

      						Do I need to use a claims management company or a law firm?
			
    

    

						

For the vast majority of consumers, there is no benefit in involving a third party in reclaiming your assets.

If you use a claims management company (CMC) or law firm to assist in the return of your assets, they will likely seek a fee which may reduce what you get back.

If you are considering using a CMC or law firm to assist with the return of your assets, we suggest you first discuss this with the trustee using the contact details provided above. 

			

  

  

            						

Protecting yourself from scams

Fraudsters sometimes claim to be from legitimate firms authorised by us, or (in the case of bankruptcy) the appointed trustee.

Be wary of fraudsters pretending to be Abacus, Arthur Temlett or the trustee and asking you to pay money to get your money back.

If you get an unexpected call from someone claiming to be Abacus, Arthur Temlett or the trustee you should:

End the call straight away.

Call them back using the phone numbers above.

Find out how to protect yourself from scams, including recovery room scams.
