title: Credit card debt ticks up
snippet: Consumers have been grappling with rising credit card interest rates and ballooning balances in the past few years, a recent Fed survey found.
fullText:
An article from
        
    

        

                Dive Brief
        

                

Consumers have been grappling with rising credit card interest rates and ballooning balances in the past few years, a recent Fed survey found.

        

            

        Published Oct. 16, 2026
    

                        

                            

                                
                            

                

                

    
        

        

    
        
            Getty Images
        
    
    
    

Dive Brief:

Between 2022 and 2025, the average U.S. household credit card debt rose by $150, or 5%, to $3,100, according to the Federal Reserve Board’s triennial Survey of Consumer Finances released last Friday. During the same period, the median figure for that U.S. credit card debt — as in the value in the middle of the set — jumped by $1,300 to $8,000, the report showed.

The share of survey respondents who owned transaction accounts, including prepaid debit cards, checking accounts and savings accounts, remained at 98.7% in 2025, about the same as in 2022 at 98.6%. However, the median value of those accounts dipped 6% between 2022 and 2025 to $8,200, the survey of 4,367 families found.

“Families were more likely to be behind on their financial obligations than at any point since the 2010 survey,” the report said. “Between the 2022 and 2025 surveys, the share of families that reported being behind on loan payments sharply increased from about 12 percent to almost 20 percent,” the report said. “Furthermore, more than 8 percent reported being two months late or more, up from 5 percent in 2022.”

Dive Insight:

During the same 2022 to 2025 period, the average credit card interest rate jumped from 14.6% to 21.4%, according to the report.

While some credit cardholders are watching their balances balloon over time, others merely use the payment tool for convenience without carrying a balance, according to the report. 

The proportion of families reporting a credit card balance after their last payment declined slightly from 45.2% in 2022 to 44.7% in 2025.

The share of survey respondents who used credit cards without carrying a balance remained about the same, at 55.8% in 2025, compared with 55.7% in 2022. Still, that proportion is lower than 64% who said the same in 2013, per the report. 

The Fed’s latest survey builds on previous research indicating that consumers rely heavily on debit and credit cards. 

In the Fed’s triennial payments study, debit cards accounted for the majority of noncash payments, totaling 120.6 billion in 2024. But while debit card usage grew at the slowest rate over the previous three years, credit card transactions exceeded debit card growth during that same period, per the study. 

As the Fed tracks rising credit card debt and interest rates, other reports signal growing strain among credit cardholders. 

The share of financially unhealthy credit cardholders ticked up from 56% last year to 60% this year, according to a J.D. Power survey released in August. Roughly three in 10 respondents in that survey with credit card debt had a balance of $2,500 or more.

On 15 October 2026, ePayments Systems Limited (EPS) entered special administration. Mark Boast and Allister Manson of Opus Restructuring LLP (Opus) have been appointed as joint special administrators. 

  

            						

EPS is authorised by the FCA to issue e-money under the Electronic Money Regulations 2011 (EMRs).

See details on the Financial Services Register.

Who to contact

The special administrators are responsible for managing customer claims against the firm and returning funds to customers where possible.

If you have any questions about the administration process, please contact the special administrators:

Email: [email protected]

Website: opusllp.com

As the firm continues to be authorised by us, we will engage with the special administrators and seek the best outcome for customers. 

          

        

Information for EPS customers

    

      

      						What is special administration?
			
    

    

						

The Payment and Electronic Money Institution Insolvency Regulations 2021 introduced a special administration regime for payment and e-money institutions.

This is similar to an ordinary administration, with additional objectives of returning customer funds as soon as reasonably practicable and ensuring timely engagement with payment systems operators and the authorities, including the FCA.

			

  

      

      						What should I do if I have money with EPS?
			
    

    

						

If you’re concerned or have any questions, contact the special administrators for help or updates.  

Email: [email protected]

The special administrators will gather information from creditors and customers about payments made to, or owed by, EPS and will provide more information on how to make a claim in due course.  

Customers can also contact our Consumer Helpline for more information. 

			

  

      

      						Is the FCA overseeing the special administration?
			
    

    

						

The special administrators are now responsible for EPS, but it continues to be FCA authorised and remains subject to our rules.  The special administrators are officers of the court and must comply with insolvency law.

They have statutory objectives, including engaging with relevant authorities such as the FCA and we will continue working with them during the special administration. 

			

  

      

      						Do I need to use a third party to get my money back? 
			
    

    

						

If you are approached by a company offering to help you recover your money, you should proceed with caution. 

For most of the firm’s clients, there will be no benefit in involving a third party in making a claim.    

If you have any questions about the special administration process, please contact the special administrators using the contact details above.  

			

  

  

            						

Being alert to scams

All customers should remain alert to the possibility of fraud.

If you are contacted unexpectedly by someone claiming to be from EPS, Opus or the FCA, you should end the call and contact them directly using verified contact details.

Find out more about protecting yourself from scams.

title: Fiserv ‘reset’ bolsters case, litigants say
snippet: The processing giant has no basis for a shareholder lawsuit to be dismissed, given its own comments, investors suing the company told a judge this week.
fullText:
Dive Brief:

Fiserv falsely portrayed customer demand and revenue growth to investors until an October 2025 organizational reset exposed the payment processor’s true financial state, shareholders suing the payments giant said in a Tuesday court filing.

Fiserv’s efforts to boost growth of its Clover point-of-sale system resulted in “an undisclosed battery of temporary cash grabs” from 2023 to 2025 designed “to create the façade of skyrocketing organic growth tied to Clover,” the plaintiffs wrote in their opposition to Fiserv’s August motion to dismiss the lawsuit. In reality, “hyperinflation in Argentina was Fiserv’s most important growth driver” during this period, the plaintiffs’ lawyers wrote.

“Defendants lied about Fiserv’s organic revenue growth in a ploy to artificially inflate the Company’s stock price for their own benefit,” according to the plaintiffs. “Defendants were strongly incentivized to commit fraud to enrich themselves” through their executive compensation plan, they added. 

Dive Insight:

The shareholder lawsuit in U.S. District Court in New York City dates to July 2025. Besides Fiserv, the lawsuit names as defendants former CEOs Frank Bisignano and Mike Lyons, along with Bob Hau, the former chief financial officer, and John Gibbons, the former head of Fiserv’s financial institutions group. 

Bisignano left Fiserv before the lawsuit landed, in May 2025, when he was confirmed by the Senate to lead the Social Security Administration after being nominated to the post by President Donald Trump in late 2024. 

A few months after Bisignano’s exit in October last year, Lyons overhauled the company’s management team and pursued what he called “a critical and necessary reset” for the payments processor. But then this year, Lyons also resigned, in June, to lead Truist Financial.

About 90% of the individual defendants’ income was tied to meeting specific targets, according to the plaintiffs. Bisignano made about $700 million in July 2025 from “illicit stock sales at inflated prices,” according to the plaintiffs’ filing on Tuesday. 

In the motion to dismiss, Milwaukee-based Fiserv defended Bisignano by saying he sold his Fiserv stock as part of an ethics agreement following his nomination to serve in the Trump administration.

The lawsuit aims to represent Fiserv shareholders as a class of litigants, from Feb. 6, 2024 to Oct. 28, 2025, according to an amended complaint filed in June. Fiserv stock declined 73% during that period, erasing about $92 billion in market capitalization, according to the lawsuit. 

“Defendants misleadingly portrayed Fiserv as a customer centric financial services provider with stable and predictable double-digit organic revenue growth that reflected genuine product strength and customer demand — artificially inflating” the stock price during the 20-month period ending last October, according to the plaintiffs’ filing Tuesday. 

Fiserv argued in its August motion that plaintiffs were displeased by the stock’s steep fall, but could not prove any alleged securities fraud because none had occurred.

Nonetheless, the defendants created “the appearance of growth” using “a fraudulent scheme” that involved “unsustainable hyperinflation” in Argentina, which boosted prices and resulting revenue from the local currency’s decline, the plaintiffs wrote. 

The plaintiffs also contend that Fiserv forced merchants to convert to the Clover point-of-sale system from its older Payeezy system, and classified them as new customers, according to the filing. 

On Tuesday, Fiserv said in a press release that this year its Clover POS system had topped 5 million device shipments globally, including 2 million over the past three years. Fiserv acquired Clover in 2019 as part of its $22 billion acquisition of First Data, where Bisignano was chief executive.

The company also diverted resources from its core banking business “to maintain the false appearance of meteoric growth” in its merchant solutions segment. That effort caused banking customers “to flee in droves,” according to the plaintiffs.

Most of Fiserv’s share decline occurred in October 2025 after Lyons announced the reset for the company, to rebuild customer relationships and improve operations. The management shift came as the company reported disappointing third-quarter results last year and reduced its earnings and revenue growth forecast.

As a result of that news, Wall Street analysts who cover the company sharply revised downward their views of the company’s growth prospects and stock price. 

The lawsuit is led by Ethenea Independent Investors SA of Luxembourg, an investment firm, and the City of Hollywood Police Officers’ Retirement System. A pension plan for retired employees of Pontiac, Michigan is also a plaintiff. The lawsuit includes a separate complaint filed in Wisconsin that a federal judge incorporated into the Manhattan case earlier this year.

Fiserv has until Nov. 12 to reply to the plaintiffs’ comments about the dismissal motion.

title: Visa, Mastercard urge court to approve fee settlement
snippet: The card networks contend Walmart and trade groups want to scuttle a legal pact over card swipe fees using recycled arguments the court has rejected.
fullText:
An article from
        
    

        

                Dive Brief
        

                

The card networks contend Walmart and trade groups want to scuttle a legal pact over card swipe fees using recycled arguments the court has rejected.

        

            

        Published Oct. 16, 2026
    

                        

                            

                                
                            

                

                

    
        

        

    
            
                A federal judge in Brooklyn, New York will convene a hearing next month to weigh final approval of a settlement between a class of 12 million merchants and card networks Visa and Mastercard.
            
        
            Getty Images
        
    
    
    

Dive Brief:

Visa and Mastercard contended in a court filing this week that merchants seeking to derail approval of a legal settlement over card swipe fees are recycling arguments they’ve made previously, and that the court has rejected. Some of the plaintiffs also have overestimated their prospects of winning at a trial, the card networks said.

Even if merchants were to win the case, “it remains unlikely that the Court would order remedies anywhere near as extreme as those the objectors claim they want, particularly given their harmful effects on cardholders and on internetwork competition,” Visa and Mastercard attorneys wrote Wednesday in a joint reply to objections lodged against the pact. The filing comes a month before a federal judge plans to hold a final approval hearing on Nov. 16.

The card networks also told the court that several large trade associations and Walmart “constitute no more than a vocal minority objecting to the settlement,” given the class size of more than 12 million members. “It is now clear that the concerns raised at preliminary approval and reiterated by largely the same objectors at final approval are nowhere near ‘pervasive,’” the companies wrote.

Dive Insight:

“Rather than offering any factual or legal basis why the Court should revisit and reverse its findings at preliminary approval, the objections merely reprise the same arguments this Court already considered and rejected,” Visa and Mastercard wrote in their support of final court approval.

The class counsel representing merchants also filed their reply to the merchants’ objections, on Wednesday, but they did so under seal. U.S. District Judge Brian Cogan told the lawyers to articulate by Monday proposed redactions to the filing so he could assess any need for confidentiality against the right of public access.

The class lawyers and networks’ attorneys reached the proposed settlement a year ago, with Cogan granting it preliminary approval in June, finding it superior to a 2024 settlement the court rejected. The litigation dates to 2005.

The latest settlement would trim credit interchange rates by 10 basis points for five years and impose a 1.25% rate for standard consumer cards for eight years. It would also give merchants the right to decline some higher-cost branded Visa and Mastercard premium and commercial credit cards. That would be a departure from the networks’ “honor all cards” rule requiring merchants to accept all cards from the networks if they accept any cards. 

In 2024, merchants paid a 2.35% fee, on average, on Visa and Mastercard transactions, according to industry research organization Nilson Report last year.

Merchants would also gain new rights to add surcharges and offer discounts for cards as a way to steer customers away from cards with higher interchange fees. But large merchants argued that they can’t easily reject the premium cards issued by banks – which offer consumers travel and cashback rewards and carry higher fees – because they are popular with customers.

The card networks also contended that objections from the National Retail Federation and Retail Industry Leaders Associations should be discounted due to several of their member companies supporting the settlement.

“Given this context, the trade association objections should be afforded little (if any) weight, and the Court should not accept the implication that those objections reflect the views of the associations’ individual members,” Visa and Mastercard wrote.

If a trial were to move forward, the merchants would likely lose given the networks’ various arguments, Visa and Mastercard told the court. “The obstacles to achieving objectors’ preferred trial result are further compounded by the complexity of this case and the certainty that appellate litigation would follow from any judgment in favor of the class,” they said.

They also urged the court to reject Walmart’s “novel proposition” that the retailer should be allowed to opt out of the class because its inclusion constitutes an unjust taking of a legal claim.

Separately, the plaintiffs’ counsel filed an objection Thursday to a request for $36 million in legal fees from 18 merchant-plaintiffs who settled for damages from the networks in a related case over swipe fees.

That group of merchants – including Crate & Barrel Holdings, Dick’s Sporting Goods, The Gap and Yum! Brands – asked the court last month for “objector fees” for their role in helping to gain improvements for merchants between the current settlement and the one reached two years ago.

If granted, the fee award would reduce the class counsel’s proposed fees to $170 million for their work in the case.

title: JPMorgan rounds up partners
snippet: The biggest U.S. bank has been collecting payments partners to better integrate software and keep up with industry trends, among other purposes.
fullText:
JPMorgan Chase, the largest U.S. bank, has been rounding up payments partners over the past three years to help the bank better integrate with clients’ software and keep an eye on industry trends.

Those are two of the ways that Todd Manning, who leads the bank’s payments partner network, sees the collection of about 120 companies serving the purposes of JPMorgan and its clients. Some of the partners include card network Visa, point-of-sale services provider Ingenico and software company Epic Systems.

Manning joined JPMorgan earlier this year as a managing director and head of corporate development and partnerships for the bank’s payments arm. Prior to that, he was at credit card company American Express for almost 17 years, most recently as head of commercial strategy, M&A and alliances, according to his LinkedIn profile.

He spoke during an Oct. 2 interview with Payments Dive about how the JPMorgan’s payments partner network, formed in 2023, contributes to the bank’s overall business as it brings payments players, software companies and fintechs into the fold.

Editor’s note: This interview has been edited for clarity and brevity.

PAYMENTS DIVE: Tell me about the network and how the bank adds partners.

TODD MANNING: The intent was to make sure that we had access to platforms that our customers are already using, where JPMorgan can form an integration to increase customer utility of using those platforms, and also just be where our existing customers are doing business. We have over 100 partners that are part of the program right now, ranging from large-scale entities like SAP and Oracle, where we've done a lot of work to look at how we can integrate some of our payment products or some data products to just make our customers' lives easier, to some smaller early-stage fintechs where we think they’re innovating, and we'd like to be able to bring that innovation in conjunction with JPMorgan payment products to our customers. 

So, does the bank integrate its software with those platforms, or does it just help the bank become more knowledgeable about how the clients are using them?

A really straightforward example that a lot of people have experience with is with an [enterprise resource planning] relationship where a customer is making a purchase, or they're using their ERP platform, to run their day-to-day business. It's a lot more convenient if you can execute a payment from within that platform. So, we have some payment integrations that take place so that a customer doesn't need to leave that environment, go to a different platform, and then go back by having a payment integration directly inside a third party's platform that we have a trusted relationship with. We can just make our customers' workflows a little more streamlined. So that's one example. There are many others, but I'd say that's one of the most basic use cases.

Todd Manning

Permission granted by JPMorgan Chase

How big is your payments partner network staff?

We have about 30 people in the payments organization that are focused on new partnership origination, so identifying where there's innovation taking place, maybe an adjacency where we want to bring that company in and see if we could form something that would generate utility for our customers. We have a team that looks at where we'd want to make venture investments, and my team also looks at where we have merger and acquisition opportunities, so where there are technology companies that we think would be a good addition to help us accelerate our product roadmap…Probably about 75% of those employees are based around partnership and ongoing monitoring of those partners. 

Talk to me about how the bank decides to invest in some of the partners, what those dollar amounts look like, and then how the bank finds and pursues these venture investments. 

Our team is active in the venture community, trying to identify where innovation is taking place, meeting with companies. We have regular meetings with founders across fintech. We have meetings with some venture capitalists as well to understand how their portfolio is evolving and what direction they're heading when it comes to the investments themselves. We try to identify high-quality companies that we could see ourselves developing a commercial relationship with. [The bank doesn’t invest in all of its partners, but rather less than a third, Manning said.]

When the bank invests, how big are the investments?

The investments themselves are typically pretty small. It really depends on the stage of the company and the valuation. We're typically looking for non-controlling investments, and so that would be somewhere typically under a 5% equity ownership stake. [Some of the investments happened prior to 2023.]

What do the companies the bank invests in get from the partnership?

The main point is it creates a bigger alignment between the two companies and an opportunity for us to learn from each other. I think one of the biggest benefits from an early stage fintech partnering with a company like JPMorgan is that they can learn from some of the control and compliance environment things that we care about a lot… Also, as we're looking at developing these relationships, we could potentially give them access to a large number of JPMorgan customers if we get it right. So, there's a lot of work that goes into making sure that the partnership is well-structured and that we have the right level of alignment in terms of expectations for control, and that we have the opportunity to bring innovation to our clients with it.

What about the potential for the bank acquiring a partner? 

It could be a potential outcome. What we're hoping to do with the partner network is to get to know companies better, see if our customers find utility in the joint solution, and then as that relationship matures, it could turn to a point where there's a venture investment made. It could mature to a point where we think the two companies can create more value together than separate. So, it could lead down the path to an acquisition, but I wouldn't say it's something that happens frequently, but there's always a chance that that could be the outcome here.

title: Congress should examine EWA bill
snippet: “Combining employer-integrated solutions and direct-to-consumer products under a single, relaxed standard weakens consumer safety,” writes an industry executive.
fullText:
Carl Morris is the vice president of compliance at earned wage access provider FlexWage Solutions. He is based in Scottsdale, Arizona.

With federal legislation in Congress being named the Earned Wage Access Consumer Protection Act, one would expect it to closely mirror an existing opinion from the federal Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. However, that is not the case.

Below is a comparison of the CFPB opinion, issued December 22, 2025, and proposed House bill H.R. 9330, contrasting four key characteristics of each.

Carl Morris

Permission granted by FlexWage Solutions

The CFPB opinion said the actual earned wage amount must be based on verified payroll data. Providers cannot rely on worker representations, estimates or predictions. Meanwhile, H.R. 9330 allows providers to use "reasonably determined" amounts, opening the door for estimations, predictions, algorithms and gross wage approximations.

The CFPB opinion also requires recoupment through direct payroll process deduction, rather than transfers from a consumer’s personal transaction account. That's in contrast to H.R. 9330, which defines no specific recoupment process, requiring only that the timing and amount match what was disclosed to the consumer.

For overpayment remedies, the CFPB opinion strictly specifies no recourse. That means earned wage access (EWA) providers have no claim against the worker if payroll deductions are insufficient, including no right to debit personal bank accounts. H.R. 9330 takes a different tack, placing no limits on how many times a provider may attempt account debits to collect overpayments. It only prohibits formal debt collection methods, late fees, and interest.

With respect to risk assessment, the CFPB opinion explicitly prohibits directly, or indirectly, assessing the credit risk of individual workers. But H.R. 9330 does not prohibit risk assessments and implicitly permits providers to evaluate employee risk and wage ratios to set advance limits (Section 2(a)(2)(A)(i)(III)).

There are additional concerns, beyond those key differences, specifically on state law preemption. The proposed bill includes a clause that supersedes state legislation classifying EWA as a loan. This would override established state-level labor, lending and usury protections. This is ironic at a time when there are eleven public actions being taken against EWA providers.

On the issue of ineffective free options, while the bill mandates one "free" EWA option, it does not specify the delivery method for that payment. Providers can offer slow ACH transfers (1–3 days) or mandate the use of proprietary cards, offering options that most employees do not want.

Data from the Center for Responsible Lending shows that 96% of all direct-to-consumer transfers include some type of fee. EWA was designed to be an employer-sponsored benefit built on accurate payroll data, direct payroll deduction, non-recourse terms, and no credit risk assessments.

Combining employer-integrated solutions and direct-to-consumer products under a single, relaxed standard weakens consumer safety.

Congress members need to be aware of these critical differences to pass meaningful legislation that truly protects consumers.

title: Visa moves ahead in China
snippet: The card network giant said it won approval from the Chinese government to begin preparing to offer card services domestically in the country.
fullText:
An article from
        
    

        

                Dive Brief
        

                

The card network giant said it won approval from the Chinese government to begin preparing to offer card services domestically in the country.

        

            

        Published Oct. 13, 2026
    

                        

                            

                                
                            

                

                

    
        

        

    
            
                The largest U.S. card network is chasing its smaller rival, Mastercard, in seeking to offer services domestically in China.
            
        
            The image by Sean MacEntee is licensed under CC BY 2.0
        
    
    
    

Dive Brief:

Visa said Tuesday in a press release that it has won approval from the Chinese government for “an application to prepare” to begin clearing card transactions in the country.

The San Francisco-based card network, the largest in the U.S., said it will “continue its efforts to complete the process” so it can begin offering the services. 

“This marks an important milestone toward the company serving China’s domestic payments market,” the release said.

Dive Insight:

Visa CEO Ryan McInerney noted in the release that the card network had been a part of China’s payments landscape for some 40 years, given the use of its services by international card holders in the country.

“We look forward to taking the necessary steps in the process, pursuant to the [People’s Bank of China’s] regulations, to begin operating domestically in China,” McInerney said in the release.

Visa is chasing its smaller U.S. rival, Mastercard, which won approval to operate within China in 2023. Purchase, New York-based Mastercard and a Chinese counterpart formed a Beijing joint venture, called Mastercard NetsUnion Information Technology, began processing payments in 2024 for cards issued by the country’s banks, according to a press release at that time.

The U.S.-based card companies had sought since at least 2017 to gain entry to the domestic Chinese market, in the hopes of attracting banks and consumers in that populous country to their services. Having the wherewithal to sell services in the country domestically can supplement and complement the U.S. card companies’ existing cross-border services flowing through China.

Still, U.S. card companies face significant domestic competition in China. They’re up against the dominant government-backed China UnionPay, which likely has an edge in attracting Chinese banks as card issuers.

“We greatly appreciate the important role of the leaders of the United States and China in pursuing a constructive and strategically stable relationship between the world’s largest economies,” McInerney said in the release.
